items.context:
A slide says: "Sculley and colleagues showed that less than 10% of the code
in a production ML system is the model." The link they cite returns HTTP
200.

What does the paper actually say?
items.why:
Invented precision that accreted through repetition. This is why the course
insists on two separate checks, and the second is the one people skip: the
URL resolves, *and* the page contains the claim you are citing it for. A
200 is evidence of the first only. The underlying point survives without
the number, which is exactly why the number was never needed.
items.true: The figure does not appear in the paper; it says only that the ML code box is tiny in proportion to the rest of the system
false: Under 5%, so the slide has rounded in the wrong direction
10% of engineering effort rather than of code, so the units are wrong
It appears in the appendix, so the claim is right but under-cited

items.context:
Public Health England, September 2020. Test results were consolidated into
Excel templates in the legacy `.xls` format, which caps a worksheet at
65,536 rows.

What happened when a file hit the ceiling?
items.why:
15,841 positive cases went unreported for a week, and the contacts of those
people were not traced. No exception, no alert, no partial record to
notice: the failure mode was silence. This is the course's opening argument
in one incident. The model was not the problem, there was no model; the
problem was a data pipeline with a capacity limit and no check that what
went in came out.
items.true: The remaining rows were not rejected with an error; they were simply absent
false: The import failed with an error, and the backlog was reprocessed once the format was changed
The file was split automatically, and the second part was processed a day late
The rows were truncated to fit, so partial records entered the system

items.context:
Google Flu Trends screened 50 million candidate queries down to 45 and
reported a mean correlation of 0.97 across nine regions, on held-out data
excluded from every prior modeling step.

Before you look: was the validation protocol the problem?
items.why:
This is the uncomfortable one, and it is why the case is in the notes.
Held-out validation was done properly and the system still degraded, because
the world changed underneath it: search behavior was not a stable proxy for
influenza, and the relationship the model learned did not survive. Validating
well is not evidence that a system works. It is evidence that it worked on
data you already had.
items.true: No. The protocol was more disciplined than a great deal of deployed machine learning gets, and it still failed in production
false: Yes; screening 50 million candidates guarantees spurious correlations survive to the held-out set
Yes; nine regions is too few to support a correlation estimate
No, and the failure was purely an infrastructure outage rather than a modeling issue

items.context:
Engineering data differs from the datasets in a general ML tutorial in a way
that changes what you have to build. What is the difference?
items.why:
Size and noise are real and neither is the distinguishing property. What
makes engineering data different is that somebody may later have to
establish which instrument produced a number, when it was calibrated, and
what the model recommended on the basis of it. That is a requirement about
records rather than about accuracy, and no amount of model quality
substitutes for it.
items.true: It carries provenance and traceability requirements, because the outputs feed decisions with physical and safety consequences
false: It is larger, so the tooling has to scale further than a tutorial's does
It is noisier, so more of the effort goes into cleaning than into modeling
It is proprietary, so it cannot be shared and every project starts from scratch

items.context:
The 737 MAX case is often summarized as "the software was buggy."

What do the investigations say about the sensor architecture?
items.why:
The generalisable shape is not about aircraft. A system that acts on one
input has no way to notice that the input is wrong, so the failure is in the
architecture rather than in the code that ran correctly on bad data. Ask of
your own systems what a single wrong sensor reading would do, and whether
anything downstream could tell.
items.true: That the system acted on a single angle-of-attack sensor, so one faulty input had no contradiction available
false: That redundant sensors were fitted and the voting logic failed to use them
That the sensors were correct and the fault lay entirely in pilot training
That sensor data was corrupted in transit between the vane and the flight computer

items.context:
The course standardizes on `uv` for environments. What failure is that
choice preventing?
items.why:
Speed and caching are real and neither is why it is in the toolchain. Every
tool in this course is chosen against a named failure, and this one is
"your figure disagrees with your notebook and neither file records why".
L13 has that failure on the page: scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9 assign folds
differently under an identical call, and only a lockfile makes that
visible.
items.true: A result that cannot be rebuilt, because a lockfile pins what was actually installed rather than what was requested
false: Slow installs, since uv resolves and downloads faster than the alternatives
Dependency conflicts, which uv resolves where pip would fail
Disk usage, since uv shares a global cache between projects

items.context:
Where does most of the engineering effort in a deployed ML system actually
go?
items.why:
This is the claim the whole course is organized around, and the reason the
first four weeks are about storage and pipelines rather than about models.
The two case studies in this session make the same point from opposite
directions: one system failed with no model in it at all, and the other had
a well-validated model and failed anyway.
items.true: Into the data infrastructure, the evaluation, and the operational practice around the model
false: Into model selection and hyperparameter tuning, which is where accuracy is won
Into inference optimization, since serving cost dominates the lifetime budget
Into user interface work, since adoption determines whether a model delivers value

sequence.prompt: Name the stages of an engineering ML system, in the order the lecture names them.
sequence.why: That is the order the lecture names them in. What is not worth believing is that the work runs left to right: reading it as a linear process is the first thing the notes tell you to unlearn. Real systems iterate hard between features and evaluation, and monitoring feeds back into acquisition the moment drift shows up in production.

terms.prompt: Stages of an engineering ML system

items.context:
Open [`l01-reproducibility.ipynb`](../lectures/l01/l01-reproducibility.ipynb)
and run it top to bottom. It is deliberately defective.

One cell fails for you and a different one fails for your neighbor. Why?
items.why:
`np.trapz` was removed in NumPy 2.0 and `np.trapezoid` was added there, so
exactly one cell fails whichever version you installed, and comparing
failures with a neighbor is the discussion. The absolute path is one of
the other two deliberate defects and it fails for everybody, which is why it
is the less interesting one: a defect that only fires on some machines is
the kind that reaches production.
items.true: It integrates a curve twice, once with `np.trapz` and once with `np.trapezoid`, and exactly one exists in your NumPy version
false: Random seeds differ between machines, so the split is different
The absolute path only exists on the author's machine, so everyone fails identically there
Cell execution order differs, so the failure depends on how you ran it

items.context:
Your model's accuracy is unchanged on the test set, but users report it has
got worse over the last quarter.

What is the most likely explanation, and where does the response belong?
items.why:
This is Google Flu Trends in miniature, and it is why "validating well is
not evidence that a system works" is a section heading rather than an
aside. A frozen test set is exactly right for comparing versions and tells
you nothing about whether the world it was drawn from still exists. L23
turns this into instrumentation.
items.true: The world moved and the frozen test set did not, so the response is monitoring the input distribution rather than re-scoring the same data
false: The users are wrong; a stable test score means stable behavior
The model has degraded numerically, so retraining on the same data will restore it
The test set has leaked into training, which inflates the score while real performance falls

items.context:
"We locked the environment, pinned the seed, and tracked the run, so the
result is trustworthy."

What does that argument miss?
items.why:
Reproducibility makes a result *checkable*; it is a precondition for
catching errors, not a substitute for doing so. Note how the Duke errors
were actually caught: not by re-running the original code, which would have
reproduced its mistakes, but by outside statisticians re-implementing the
analysis from scratch and finding the two disagreed. Reproduction confirms
you can regenerate a number. Confirming it is right is a separate act
called validation.
items.true: Reproducible is not the same as correct: a pipeline with an off-by-one error will reproduce the wrong answer with perfect fidelity
false: Nothing, provided the lockfile is regenerated whenever a dependency changes
Seeds do not make a result reproducible across platforms, so the claim overstates what pinning buys
Tracking is only meaningful if the tracked run is also deployed, which this does not say

items.context:
A lockfile pins the exact version of every Python package. What does it
still not pin?
items.why:
A package version is not the same as the code that runs. The lockfile says
nothing about system C libraries, the CUDA toolkit, or the operating system,
and a pinned version can even become unavailable if it is removed from the
index. For most engineering work that is enough; when you need the whole
stack frozen the tool is a container, which is a Week 12 topic. The honest
framing is that `uv` gives you a reproducible Python environment, which is
most of what you need and not quite all of it.
items.true: The compiled bytes: platform-specific wheels differ between macOS and Linux, and system C libraries are not covered at all
false: The random seed, which has to be set separately in code
Transitive dependencies, which resolve freshly on each install
The Python interpreter version, which is recorded separately

sequence.prompt: The uv commands of a normal day, in the order you reach for them.
sequence.why: init creates the project, add resolves and locks a dependency, run executes inside the environment after checking the lockfile still matches pyproject.toml, and sync rebuilds the whole thing from the lockfile on a machine that has never seen it. The last one is the one that ends "works on my machine".

items.context:
Twenty minutes of poking at a file to decide whether an idea is worth
pursuing. Should you set up a locked, tracked, packaged project first?
items.why:
There is a real judgment call about when to pay for the discipline. Full
scaffolding on a twenty-minute exploration is cumbersome and is its own kind
of over-engineering. The moment an analysis will be rerun, shared, built
upon, or believed by anyone, including your future self, it has crossed the
line, and almost nobody notices the crossing at the time. So the default
leans toward scaffolding, because retrofitting is the expensive direction.
items.true: No for a genuinely throwaway exploration, but the trap is that results cross the line into needing it quietly
false: Yes, always; the discipline is cheap and retrofitting is expensive
No; scaffolding is only warranted once a result is going to be published
Yes, because an unlocked environment cannot produce a result worth acting on at all

items.context:
A content hash tells you two runs used different data. What does it not
tell you?
items.why:
A hash is a smoke alarm, not an investigation. Detecting change is the
floor of data provenance rather than the ceiling, and the tools that go
further, versioning data by content with a readable history of what changed
and why, are `git-lfs` and DVC. Collisions are not the concern: the hash is
certain that the file differs, and useless about everything after that.
items.true: Which rows changed, whether the change was a fix or a corruption, or whether it matters
false: Whether the file is genuinely different, since hashes collide in practice
When the change happened, which requires a timestamp alongside the hash
Who made the change, which requires an audit log rather than a hash

items.context:
Every run in your MLflow project logs a seed. A colleague concludes the
project is reproducible.

What is wrong with that inference?
items.why:
The tracker is a filing system, and a filing system is only as trustworthy
as the discipline of the person filing. Logging a seed documents one input
to a run that may still be irreproducible for a dozen other reasons. The
third option is a real and separate concern; it is not the flaw in the
inference, which is that recording is being mistaken for guaranteeing.
items.true: Tracking records, it does not enforce: MLflow will faithfully log a run whose environment was never locked
false: Nothing; a logged seed plus logged parameters is what reproducibility means in practice
Seeds are per-library, so one logged seed does not cover NumPy, PyTorch and Python's own RNG
The seed should be logged as a tag rather than a parameter, or it will not be searchable

items.context: Why do large binary files not belong in plain git?
items.why:
Code, data, and models are three different versioning problems and the
session is explicit that one tool does not serve all three. Git is superb
for text it can diff and terrible for a 400 MB file rewritten weekly,
because every version stays in the history forever. That the diffs are
uninformative is true and is not the binding cost; the binding cost is that
the repository stops being clonable.
items.true: Git stores a full copy of every version, so a repeatedly-changed binary makes the history unusable to clone
false: Git rejects files above a fixed size limit, so they cannot be committed at all
Git cannot compute diffs for binary content, so the commits carry no information
Binary files break the working tree on checkout across operating systems

items.context:
What is the point of turning an exploratory notebook into a module with a
command-line entry point?
items.why:
Notebooks are version-controllable, awkwardly, so that is not the argument.
The argument is that a notebook's execution order is a human decision made
at runtime, and a module's is not. Once there is an entry point, CI can run
it, a scheduler can run it, and a test can assert what it produces, none of
which is available to a sequence of cells.
items.true: It becomes testable and callable, so the thing you validated can be run again by something other than a human clicking cells
false: Speed, since a script runs faster than the same code in a notebook kernel
Notebooks cannot be version-controlled, so moving to a script is what makes the work reviewable
It reduces memory use, since a script releases state between stages

sequence.prompt: The notebook refactor: the functions the data moves through, in order.
sequence.why: The refactor is mechanical, which is the good news. Each function takes its inputs as arguments and returns a value, so it can be imported and tested on its own rather than depending on the ambient state of a notebook that has to be run in an order you remember.

terms.prompt: Folders and files of the src layout

items.context:
Two labs report different results from what is supposedly the same
analysis. Both can reproduce their own numbers exactly.

What resolves it?
items.why:
Every other option is a good diagnostic and none of them can catch a shared
misunderstanding of what the analysis should do. Re-running reproduces;
re-implementing validates. The Duke errors survived because re-running the
original code would have faithfully regenerated the mistakes, and they were
only found when outside statisticians built the analysis again from scratch
and the two versions disagreed.
items.true: Re-implementing the analysis independently, which is how the Duke errors were actually found
false: Comparing lockfiles, since a dependency difference is the likeliest cause of a numeric disagreement
Re-running each pipeline on the other lab's data, which isolates data from code
Increasing precision, since disagreements of this kind usually trace to floating-point accumulation

items.context:
Open [`l02-scaffold.ipynb`](../lectures/l02/l02-scaffold.ipynb) and work
through building the project scaffold.

What does `uv` produce that a `requirements.txt` does not?
items.why:
A requirements file is a request; a lockfile is a record. The distinction
only bites when a transitive dependency moves under you, which is exactly
the failure L13 documents when scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9 assigned folds
differently under an identical call. Speed is real and is not the reason
this is in the toolchain.
items.true: A lockfile recording what was actually installed, including transitive dependencies, rather than what was asked for
false: A faster install, since uv resolves dependencies in parallel
A virtual environment, which requirements.txt cannot create
A dependency graph, which requirements.txt flattens and loses

items.context:
```sql
SELECT * FROM readings WHERE value <> 30;
```
Your sensor table has nulls in `value`. What does this return?
items.why:
SQL has three truth values, not two: true, false, and unknown. "Unknown is
not equal to 30" evaluates to unknown rather than to true, so the row is
not returned. This is defined semantics rather than a defect, and it
quietly produces wrong analyses for anyone who forgets it. The same family
contains a worse one: `NOT IN` against a subquery containing a single null
returns no rows at all.
items.true: Every row whose value is not 30, silently excluding all null rows
false: Every row whose value is not 30, including the null ones, since null is not 30
An error, since a comparison against null is not permitted in a WHERE clause
Every row, since null comparisons default to true in PostgreSQL

items.context:
A mote dropped half its readings. You compute `avg(value)` over its rows.
What do you get?
items.why:
`count(*)` counts rows while `count(value)` counts only non-null ones, and
`avg(value)` averages only the readings that are present. So the mote is
not penalized in the average unless you have separately counted how many it
reported. The habit worth forming is to carry a completeness count next to
any aggregate over sensor data, because the aggregate alone cannot tell you
whether it summarizes everything or half of it.
items.true: An average over the readings that are present, with the missing ones simply absent from it
false: An average that treats missing readings as zero, biasing it downward
Null, because any aggregate over a column containing nulls is null
An error, unless the nulls are filtered out first

items.context:
Your experiment metadata records a different, unpredictable set of fields
for every run. You are putting it in PostgreSQL and the schema keeps
changing.

What does that tell you?
items.why:
The same schema that protected your readings table is expensive to change
once it is large, and a migration against a nine-million-row table in a live
deployment is a real operation with real risk. Heterogeneous metadata is the
case where rigidity stops paying, and recognizing it is the point: the
relational model is a default, not a universal answer. A JSON column is a
genuine option and it is the relational model conceding the argument rather
than winning it.
items.true: That this is exactly the territory where the rigid schema stops helping and document stores earn their place
false: That the schema needs a JSON column, which restores flexibility inside the relational model
That the runs should be normalized further, into a table per field type
That migrations should be automated, since the schema churn is a tooling problem

items.context:
Why store sensor data long (one row per reading) rather than wide (one
column per sensor)?
items.why:
A wide table encodes your current instrument list into the schema, so
commissioning a sensor becomes a migration and decommissioning one leaves a
column of nulls forever. Long tables decouple the two. The cost is real and
worth knowing: queries that want several channels side by side now need a
pivot or a join, which is why the session spends time on window functions
and time bucketing.
items.true: Adding a sensor is a new row rather than a schema change, and the schema stops depending on which instruments exist
false: Long tables compress better, so the storage cost is lower at scale
Long tables are faster to query, since the index fits in memory
Wide tables cannot represent timestamps consistently across sensors

items.context:
"We used a timestamp column, so the times are correct."

What did 30 June 2012 demonstrate?
items.why:
The case is in the notes because a type that carries physical meaning has
to cope with how the physical quantity actually behaves, and time is the one
everybody assumes is simple. Timezones are a real hazard and a different
one. The general shape is the session's argument about types: a column
declared with the right type is carrying a claim about the world, and the
world occasionally declines to cooperate.
items.true: That a leap second is a real event a timestamp type has to survive, and systems assuming fixed-length days failed
false: That timezone conversion is the main hazard, and UTC storage solves it
That NTP drift accumulates faster than most systems account for
That millisecond precision is insufficient for high-rate sensor data

items.context:
When should a measured quantity be stored as `numeric` rather than
`double precision`?
items.why:
"Always" is the tempting answer and it is wrong: `numeric` is materially
slower and most sensor readings are approximate measurements of a
continuous quantity, where double precision is the honest representation.
The session is also blunt that this does not save you from floating point
elsewhere: a value read into Python as a float is a float again, whatever
the column said.
items.true: When exactness at the stored precision matters more than arithmetic speed, for instance for money or a regulated tolerance
false: Always, since numeric is exact and double precision is approximate
When the values span many orders of magnitude, which double precision handles poorly
Never for sensor data, since numeric cannot represent scientific notation

terms.prompt: Types this schema uses for engineering data

items.context:
A column is declared `double precision NOT NULL`. A reading arrives as
-9999, the instrument's error sentinel.

What happens?
items.why:
The type says "this is a number that is present". It says nothing about
whether the number is physically possible. Sentinels like -9999 are
extremely common in instrument data and they pass every type check, which
is why the session insists on `CHECK` constraints for range and on
validation as a separate layer. This is the same lesson as the units
assertion in L7: the declaration is not the check.
items.true: It is stored, because a typed column is still not a validated column
false: The insert is rejected, since -9999 is outside any plausible physical range
It is coerced to null, since the sentinel is recognized by the driver
It is stored and flagged, since PostgreSQL tracks out-of-range values

sequence.prompt: Loading a sensor export that resists the loader, through a staging table.
steps: COPY the raw text into a permissive table
insert into the real readings table
sequence.why: The point of the staging table is that the cleaning rules end up written down as queries anyone can read, rather than buried in a one-off script. Some of them you do not have to write at all: the foreign key to sensors rejects the corrupt mote ids for you the moment you try to insert one.

items.context:
A time-range query over a large readings table is slow. You add an index
and it is still slow.

What tells you why?
items.why:
Every other option is a real diagnostic and each answers a narrower
question. The plan is the one that tells you what the database actually
decided to do, which is frequently not what you assumed when you added the
index: a predicate that wraps the column in a function, or a range broad
enough that a sequential scan is genuinely cheaper, both produce a
correctly-ignored index.
items.true: The query plan, from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which shows whether the index was used and what it cost
false: The table statistics, which show whether the index is selective enough to help
The query duration across repeated runs, which distinguishes cold cache from a bad plan
The index size on disk, which indicates whether it fits in memory

items.context:
Open [`l03-sql-timeseries.ipynb`](../lectures/l03/l03-sql-timeseries.ipynb)
and run the same range query with and without the index, reading the plan
each time.

What changes in the plan?
items.why:
An index that exists and an index that is used are different things, and
the plan is the only place the difference is visible. This is the same
discipline as the rest of the course: the artifact exists is not the same
claim as the artifact works, and you check by looking at what actually
happened rather than at what you configured.
items.true: The scan type changes, and the plan shows whether the index was actually chosen rather than merely present
false: Only the timing; the plan is identical because the planner is deterministic
The row estimates change, since an index updates the table statistics
Nothing visible; index use is reported only in the server log
